title: Anywhere Gives AI Assistants a Map of Your Saved Places
summary: Anywhere Gives AI Assistants a Map of Your Saved Places
body_markdown:
[Anywhere](https://anywhere.fenn.chat/) is building a personal map that an AI assistant can use, not just display. The free iPhone app combines saved places, memories and friends with connections that let assistants read existing locations and add new ones. A restaurant mentioned in a conversation can become a pin instead of another recommendation buried in chat history.


The product comes from Charly Delaroche, whose launch describes a career working on maps at Zenly, amo and Life360. Anywhere, part of Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 batch, applies that experience to a different interface question: what should an assistant know about the places that already matter to its user?


The launch names ChatGPT and Instinct as connections. Rather than treating the map as the final output of a search, Anywhere makes it shared context for future conversations. An assistant can work with a collection that already exists, while additions made through chat remain available in the map.


[Watch the original Anywhere launch video](https://youtu.be/cjlvUJTQkgk)


Anywhere also has its own AI guide, Fenn. The company describes it as a way to explore locations, get suggestions and save discoveries. This gives users a route into the product without first deciding how to connect an outside assistant: the map and its conversational guide can operate as one experience.


The[App Store description](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/anywhere-your-only-map/id6823839358) fills in the more conventional pieces of that experience. Users can organize places into lists, attach ratings and private notes, and share their location with selected friends. A visit history and a map that reveals explored areas give the product a memory of movement as well as a collection of deliberate saves.


Those features serve different purposes. A saved restaurant captures intent; a visited place captures behavior; a friend’s location supplies a temporary social signal. Bringing them together could make recommendations more specific, but it also means the application handles information more personal than a generic search for nearby coffee.


The app description says users can inspect what connected agents read or change, undo changes and disconnect access. Friend location sharing is opt-in, with controls over who can see it. Automatic visit tracking requires location permission, so the richest version of the map depends on choices users make about ongoing collection.


The larger travel-planning vision is not the same as the available feature set. Delaroche describes a future in which a New York trip could be assembled from saved coffee shops, friends’ recommendations and a hotel location. The launch explicitly identifies that anticipatory planning as what the team is building next.


That distinction keeps the current pitch narrower and more concrete: preserve useful place information, make it accessible to assistants and let conversations update it. The launch does not establish that Anywhere currently books trips or autonomously produces the full itinerary described in its forward-looking example.


There are also practical steps toward making an existing collection portable. The App Store release notes describe importing Google Maps lists through shared links. That reduces the need to rebuild a personal catalogue one place at a time, particularly for someone who has already accumulated years of recommendations elsewhere.


Anywhere is available on iOS, with Android described on its website as coming soon. Its immediate test is whether a map can become a useful working memory across conversations without making users feel they have handed over an opaque location archive. The controls for inspection, reversal and disconnection are therefore part of the product’s core proposition, not merely settings around its edges.
